title: Given an array of elements, return the k elements that appear most frequently, using a hash map to count and a heap to select.
shortTitle: Find the Top K Frequent Elements
keyPoints: Phase 1: count occurrences in a HashMap with a single linear pass using merge().
Phase 2: select the top k using a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency, evicting the least frequent when the heap exceeds k.
Counting is O(n); heap selection over m distinct values is O(m log k); total is O(n + m log k).
Bucket sort by frequency achieves O(n) total because counts are bounded by n.
The heap approach is preferred when k is small; bucket sort is preferred when k is large or latency matters.
Both approaches share the identical frequency-map phase and differ only in the selection step.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count with a hash map, then keep the k highest counts in a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Frequency counting** – a single linear pass with `map.merge(element, 1, Integer::sum)` builds a count for each distinct element.
- **Min-heap selection** – a `PriorityQueue` of size k ordered by frequency keeps the k most frequent; the root (least frequent of the leaders) is evicted when a higher count arrives.
- **Bucket sort alternative** – create n+1 buckets indexed by frequency, drop each element into its count bucket, scan from highest bucket down to collect k elements in O(n).
- **Complexity** – O(n + m log k) with heap, O(n) with bucket sort, where m is the count of distinct elements.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the three most common merchant categories customers spend on. A clerk first tallies every transaction, one count per category. Then she keeps a small tray of three categories with the biggest counts, arranged so the smallest count is at the front for easy swap-out. For each new count, if it beats the front of the tray, she swaps it in. The tray holds the top three at the end.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Transactions: [UPI, NEFT, UPI, IMPS, UPI, NEFT, RTGS]   k = 2

Phase 1 - Frequency Map:
  UPI  -> 3
  NEFT -> 2
  IMPS -> 1
  RTGS -> 1

Phase 2a - Min-Heap (size k=2):
  offer UPI(3)  -> heap: [UPI(3)]
  offer NEFT(2) -> heap: [NEFT(2), UPI(3)]
  offer IMPS(1) -> heap size 3 > k=2, poll IMPS(1) -> heap: [NEFT(2), UPI(3)]
  offer RTGS(1) -> heap size 3 > k=2, poll RTGS(1) -> heap: [NEFT(2), UPI(3)]
  Result: [UPI, NEFT]

Phase 2b - Bucket Sort:
  bucket[3] = [UPI]
  bucket[2] = [NEFT]
  bucket[1] = [IMPS, RTGS]
  Scan from top: bucket[3] -> UPI, bucket[2] -> NEFT. Collected 2. Done.
  Result: [UPI, NEFT]
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Top K Frequent Elements Flow               │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                  │
│   Phase 1: Count frequencies                     │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐               │
│   │ for each element:            │               │
│   │   freq.merge(e, 1, sum)      │               │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘               │
│                │                                 │
│                ▼                                 │
│   Phase 2: Select top k                          │
│                                                  │
│   Option A: Min-Heap          Option B: Buckets  │
│   ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐    │
│   │ offer each entry │   │ bucket[count]=e  │    │
│   │ if size > k:     │   │ scan high to low │    │
│   │   poll smallest  │   │ collect k items  │    │
│   └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘    │
│                                                  │
│   Return top k elements                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the top k frequent elements splits into two phases. First, count occurrences in a single linear pass using a HashMap. Second, select the k highest counts from that map.

The min-heap approach keeps a heap of size k ordered by frequency. You offer each distinct element, and when the heap exceeds k, you poll the least frequent. After processing all entries, the heap holds the top k. This runs in O(n + m log k).

The bucket sort alternative exploits the fact that counts are bounded by n. Create n+1 buckets indexed by frequency, drop each element into its count bucket, and scan from the highest bucket down collecting k elements. That is O(n) with no log factor.

At the National Bank of India, the operations dashboard displayed the k most frequent transaction types for the day. Because daily volume was large and the dashboard had to refresh quickly, Rajesh used bucket sort for linear selection, keeping the min-heap as the fallback for streaming scenarios.

Remember one sentence: count with a HashMap, then select the top k with a size-k min-heap or bucket sort by frequency.
